To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) Adenoviral vectors activate the type I IFN immune response; (ii) the type I IFNs are crucial for efficient tumor regression; (iii) the type I response can be induced by Ad vectors in vivo; (iv) the type I and type II responses can be synergistic in the context of Ad-mediated gene transfer.

(i) the type I IFN innate immunity is induced by the Ad vector itself and (ii) the combined action of the transgene and vector-induced type I IFN contributes to the regression and clinical response of cutaneous T cell lymphoma lesions to Ad-IFNgamma gene transfer.
the innate immune response to Ad- IFN-gamma is a combination of type I and type II IFN induction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel therapeutic strategies for the treatment of cutaneous lymphoma and other malignancies.
a novel mechanism of gene therapy, which is based on the combined expression of IFN-gammas and IFN-gamma-inducible genes.
the innate immune response to Ad-mediated gene transfer and the biological consequences of this response.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the combination of IFN-alpha/IFN-gamma may be more effective than IFN-gamma alone.
Ad-IFNg gene therapy induces a combined type I and type II IFN response, and that this response is crucial in the regression of cutaneus lymphoma.

the combination of Ad vector-induced type I IFN innate response and the transgene-mediated type II IFN response to IFN-gamma is crucial for the therapeutic effect of intralesional IFN- gamma gene therapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
type I IFN innate immunity is an integral component of the antitumor response to Ad-mediated IFN-g gene transfer.
Ad-IFN gamma gene transfer induces type II and type I IFN responses in cutaneous lymphoma, which together contribute to the regression of the lesions.
Ad-IFNgamma gene transfer to lymphoma lesions results in a complex gene expression profile, which includes type I and type II IFN-inducible genes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the innate immune system can be a double-edged sword in the context of gene therapy, and its activation should be carefully considered in the design of gene transfer protocols.
the use of Ads in cancer gene therapy should be accompanied by the use of antiviral agents, which would block the induction of the type I IFN innate response.
the innate immune response to Ad vectors should be considered when using Ads for gene transfer in the clinic.
